title: How to Convert PDF to JPG Without Losing Quality
excerpt: The settings that actually matter when turning PDF pages into sharp JPG images — resolution, DPI, and compression explained in plain English.
description: Learn how to convert PDF to JPG without losing quality. Understand DPI, resolution and JPEG compression so your exported images stay crisp and readable.
author: PDF Tools Team
imageAlt: PDF document being converted into a high-quality JPG image
contentHtml:
Converting a PDF to JPG sounds simple — until the result comes out blurry, pixelated, or weirdly soft around the text. The good news is that quality loss is almost always caused by two or three settings you can control. This guide explains exactly what those settings do and how to keep your images sharp.

Why PDF-to-JPG conversion can lose quality

A PDF page is usually vector data (text and shapes described by math), so it stays crisp at any zoom level. A JPG is a raster image — a fixed grid of pixels. Converting means "rendering" the page into pixels at a chosen resolution, then compressing it. Two things decide the result:

  • Resolution / DPI — how many pixels the page is rendered into. Too few and everything looks soft.
  • JPEG compression — JPG throws away detail to shrink file size. Push it too hard and you get blocky "artifacts" around text and edges.

Pick the right resolution (DPI)

DPI (dots per inch) is the single biggest factor. As a rule of thumb:

  • 72–96 DPI — fine for on-screen thumbnails and previews.
  • 150 DPI — a good default for sharing or viewing on screens.
  • 300 DPI — print quality; use this when the JPG will be printed or zoomed.

If your tool offers a scale slider instead of a DPI box, higher scale = higher resolution. Doubling the scale roughly doubles the pixel dimensions (and the file size).

Set JPEG quality to 85–95%

JPEG quality is a trade-off between file size and fidelity. For documents with text, stay in the 85–95% range. Below ~80% you'll start to see fuzzy halos around letters. At 100% the file gets large with almost no visible benefit, so 90% is usually the sweet spot.

Tip: If sharp text matters more than file size — for example a scanned contract — consider exporting to PNG instead. PNG is lossless and never adds compression artifacts.

Step-by-step

  1. Open the PDF to JPG converter and drag your PDF onto the drop zone.
  2. Set the resolution to 150 DPI for screen use or 300 DPI for print.
  3. Set JPEG quality to around 90%.
  4. Convert, then check one page at 100% zoom before downloading the rest.

Because this tool runs entirely in your browser, your PDF is never uploaded to a server — the rendering happens on your own device, which is both private and fast.

Frequently asked questions

Why does my converted JPG look blurry?

Almost always low DPI. Re-export at 150 or 300 DPI and the text will sharpen up immediately.

Is JPG or PNG better for scanned documents?

PNG, if you want perfectly crisp text and don't mind a larger file. JPG is better when you need smaller files and the page contains photos.

Will converting reduce the original PDF's quality?

No. You're creating new image files; the original PDF is untouched.

title: PDF to PNG vs PDF to JPG: Which Should You Use?
excerpt: JPG is smaller, PNG is sharper. Here's a simple decision guide for choosing the right format for documents, screenshots, and photos.
description: PDF to PNG or PDF to JPG? Compare file size, transparency, and text sharpness so you choose the right image format every time.
author: PDF Tools Team
imageAlt: Side by side comparison of PNG and JPG image formats
contentHtml:
When you export a PDF page as an image, you'll usually be asked to choose between JPG and PNG. They look similar, but under the hood they behave very differently. Picking the right one saves you from blurry text or bloated files.

The one-line summary

Use JPG for photos and smaller files. Use PNG for text, screenshots, line art, and anything that needs transparency. Everything below is just the reasoning behind that rule.

How they compress

JPG uses lossy compression — it discards detail your eye is unlikely to miss, which makes files small but can blur sharp edges. PNG uses lossless compression — nothing is thrown away, so edges stay crisp, but files are larger.

Side-by-side comparison

  • Text & sharp edges: PNG wins. JPG can add halos around letters.
  • Photographs: JPG wins. It compresses smooth gradients efficiently with no visible loss.
  • File size: JPG is typically 3–10× smaller for the same page.
  • Transparency: Only PNG supports it. JPG always has a solid background.
  • Re-saving repeatedly: PNG is safe; JPG degrades a little each time it's re-compressed.

Real-world examples

A scanned contract you'll email: PNG if legibility is critical, JPG at 90% if size matters more.

A page that's mostly a photograph: JPG, every time.

A logo or diagram you'll place on a coloured background: PNG, for the transparency.

How to convert either way

  1. Open the converter and drop in your PDF.
  2. Choose PDF to JPG for small files or PDF to PNG for maximum sharpness.
  3. Set the resolution (150 DPI for screen, 300 DPI for print) and convert.

Both conversions happen locally in your browser, so your files never leave your device.

Frequently asked questions

Is PNG always higher quality than JPG?

For text and sharp graphics, yes. For photographs the visible difference is tiny while PNG files are far larger.

Can I convert JPG to PNG later?

You can, but it won't restore detail JPG already discarded. Start from the format you ultimately need.

title: How to Compress a PDF for Free Without Losing Quality
excerpt: Email bouncing because your PDF is too big? Here's how PDF compression works and how to shrink files in your browser without wrecking quality.
description: Compress large PDF files for free, right in your browser. Learn what makes PDFs huge and how to reduce file size while keeping text readable.
author: PDF Tools Team
imageAlt: Large PDF file being compressed into a smaller file
contentHtml:
Most "file too large" errors come down to one thing: images embedded in the PDF at far higher resolution than they need to be. Compression fixes that. Here's what's actually happening and how to do it safely.

Why PDFs get so big

A PDF that's mostly text is tiny. The size balloons when it contains:

  • High-resolution scanned pages (a scanner often saves at 600 DPI).
  • Embedded photos saved at full camera resolution.
  • Fonts embedded multiple times, or uncompressed image data.

How PDF compression works

A compressor re-encodes the images inside the PDF: it downsamples them to a sensible resolution (say 150 DPI) and applies efficient compression. Text and vector graphics stay sharp because they aren't images — only the heavy bitmap content is reduced.

Key idea: You're not lowering the quality of the document, you're removing resolution you can't see anyway. A 600 DPI scan viewed on a screen looks identical at 150 DPI but is a fraction of the size.

How much can you save?

Image-heavy PDFs commonly drop by 50–90%. A 25 MB scanned report can often land under 5 MB — comfortably within most email limits (Gmail's cap is 25 MB).

Step-by-step

  1. Open the PDF compressor and drop your file in.
  2. Pick a compression level. Medium is a good balance; high squeezes hardest.
  3. Compress, then open the result and check the smallest text is still readable.

Everything runs in your browser, so even confidential documents stay on your machine.

Tips for the best results

  • If a scan is still huge, the original was probably scanned at very high DPI — compress harder.
  • For documents you'll print, keep at least 150 DPI; for screen-only, 96–120 DPI is plenty.
  • Need it even smaller? Split out the pages you don't need with a PDF splitter first.

Frequently asked questions

Will compression make my text blurry?

No — text is vector data and isn't affected. Only embedded images are downsampled.

Is it safe for sensitive documents?

Yes. Because the compression happens locally in your browser, your file is never uploaded anywhere.

title: How to Convert JPG to PDF: A Complete Guide
excerpt: Turn one image or a whole stack of photos into a single, tidy PDF — with the right page size, orientation, and order.
description: Convert JPG images to PDF the right way. Combine multiple photos into one document, control page size and order, all free and in your browser.
author: PDF Tools Team
imageAlt: Several JPG photos being combined into a single PDF document
contentHtml:
Converting images to PDF is the easiest way to send a clean, single-file version of receipts, ID photos, or a multi-page document you photographed with your phone. Here's how to do it well.

Why convert JPG to PDF at all?

  • One file instead of many — recipients get a single tidy document, not a dozen attachments.
  • Consistent layout — pages keep their order and orientation when opened anywhere.
  • Universal format — PDF opens identically on every device and is the standard for official submissions.

Before you convert: prep your images

A little prep makes a big difference:

  • Order them — rename files 01, 02, 03… so they appear in the right sequence.
  • Rotate any sideways photos first so the PDF isn't rotated.
  • Crop out backgrounds for documents you photographed at an angle.

Step-by-step

  1. Open the JPG to PDF converter.
  2. Select or drag in all your images at once.
  3. Drag to reorder pages if needed.
  4. Choose page size (A4 or Letter) and orientation.
  5. Convert and download your single PDF.

Choosing page size and fit

For documents, A4 (or Letter in the US) with "fit image to page" gives clean, printable results. For photos you want edge-to-edge, choose a fit option that matches the image's aspect ratio so you don't get large white borders.

Tip: If the final PDF is large, run it through a PDF compressor afterwards — phone photos are high-resolution and add up quickly.

Frequently asked questions

Can I combine images of different sizes?

Yes. Use a consistent page size with "fit to page" so every image is scaled neatly onto the same dimensions.

Will the quality drop?

No noticeable loss — your images are placed into the PDF at full quality. Only compressing the PDF afterwards reduces size.

Are my photos uploaded anywhere?

No. The conversion runs entirely in your browser, so your images stay on your device.

title: How to Merge & Split PDF Files Safely
excerpt: Combine several PDFs into one, or pull out just the pages you need — without sending sensitive documents to a stranger's server.
description: Learn how to merge multiple PDFs into one file and split out specific pages safely in your browser, with no uploads and no quality loss.
author: PDF Tools Team
imageAlt: PDF pages being merged together and split apart
contentHtml:
Merging and splitting are the two most common PDF chores: stitching several files into one, or extracting just the pages that matter. Both are quick — and you don't have to upload private documents to do them.

Why privacy matters here

Many free online PDF tools upload your file to their servers to process it. For a restaurant menu that's fine; for a signed contract, a bank statement, or medical records, it's a real risk. Browser-based tools do all the work on your own device, so the document never leaves your computer.

Merging PDFs into one file

  1. Open the PDF merger.
  2. Add all the PDFs you want to combine.
  3. Drag them into the order you want — this becomes the page order.
  4. Merge and download the single combined file.

Common uses: combining a cover letter and CV, assembling scanned pages into one report, or merging monthly statements into a single archive.

Splitting a PDF

Splitting lets you keep only what you need:

  • Extract a page range — e.g. pages 5–8 of a long report.
  • Pull out a single page — like one form from a packet.
  • Break a big file into parts — handy before emailing.

    • Open the PDF splitter, choose the pages or ranges, and download the result.

    Tip: Merge first, then split, if you're reorganising several documents — combine everything, then extract the final sequence you want.

    Does merging or splitting reduce quality?

    No. These operations copy the existing page data exactly — text stays selectable and images stay at their original resolution. Nothing is re-compressed.

    Frequently asked questions

    Is there a page limit?

    No fixed limit, though very large files depend on your device's memory. For huge documents, split in stages.

    Will the bookmarks and links survive?

    Page content, text and images are preserved. Complex interactive features can vary, so check the result if your PDF has forms.

title: How to Convert HEIC to JPG (iPhone, Mac & Windows)
excerpt: Why your iPhone photos won't open on some apps — and the fastest free way to turn HEIC files into universally compatible JPGs.
description: iPhone photos saved as HEIC won't open everywhere. Learn how to convert HEIC to JPG for free on any device, with no quality loss and no uploads.
author: PDF Tools Team
imageAlt: HEIC photo from an iPhone converting to a JPG image
contentHtml:
You AirDrop a photo from your iPhone, try to open it on a Windows PC or upload it to an older website, and… nothing. The culprit is usually HEIC — Apple's modern photo format. Here's why it happens and how to fix it in seconds.

What is HEIC, and why does it cause problems?

HEIC (High Efficiency Image Container) is the format iPhones use by default. It stores photos at roughly half the size of JPG with the same quality — great for your storage, but not every app or website understands it yet. JPG, by contrast, opens literally everywhere.

The quick fix: convert to JPG

Converting HEIC to JPG makes the photo universally compatible. You lose the storage efficiency, but you gain the ability to open and share it anywhere.

On any device (easiest)

  1. Open the HEIC to JPG converter.
  2. Drag in one photo or a whole batch.
  3. Convert and download the JPG versions.

This works the same on iPhone, Android, Mac, and Windows because it runs in your browser — and your photos are never uploaded to a server.

Stop iPhone from saving HEIC in the first place

If you'd rather avoid converting every time, change the capture format on your iPhone:

  1. Open Settings → Camera → Formats.
  2. Choose Most Compatible — your iPhone will now shoot JPG instead of HEIC.

The trade-off is larger photo files, so only switch if compatibility matters more than storage.

Tip: Converting a HEIC to JPG slightly increases file size because JPG is less efficient. If you then need a smaller file for the web, resize or compress the JPG afterwards.

Frequently asked questions

Does converting HEIC to JPG lose quality?

There's a tiny, usually invisible loss because JPG re-compresses the image. For everyday sharing it's not noticeable.

Can I convert many HEIC photos at once?

Yes — batch convert the whole set and download them together.

Will I lose the photo's date or location data?

Basic image data is preserved during conversion, though some apps strip location metadata for privacy when exporting.
